oneliner.t: Two-term Republican congressman from Tucson (since January 2023), a Mexican-born naturalized citizen and former senior adviser to Gov. Doug Ducey, on House Appropriations, seeking a third term against Democrat JoAnna Mendoza in toss-up AZ-06.

born.note: Birthplace in both; date from Wikipedia only.

upbringing.t: Born in Hermosillo, he came to Tucson as a young boy with his parents and two younger sisters through a port of entry; the family became lawful permanent residents with help from their church. His father drove a bus. He attended Tucson public schools (Rincon High School), Pima Community College and the University of Arizona, working maintenance and fast-food jobs, and was the first in his family to graduate from college. He worked for the University of Arizona and the Tucson Hispanic Chamber of Commerce, then as a senior adviser to Gov. Doug Ducey and vice chair of the Arizona-Mexico Commission (2015–2021). He and his wife Laura have six children.

profile.office_note: U.S. House since Jan. 3, 2023. His Arizona-Mexico Commission vice chair role (2015–2021) was an appointed post on a governor's commission and is listed under career, not counted here.

career.role: Intern, then fellow (Rep. Ed Pastor, D; Rep. Loretta Sanchez, D)
Membership director; vice president of outreach
Senior adviser to Gov. Doug Ducey; vice chair, Arizona-Mexico Commission
career.org: Office of the Governor of Arizona

career.role: U.S. Representative, AZ-06 (Appropriations — vice chair, Homeland Security subcommittee; National Security, State & Related Programs subcommittee; Veterans' Affairs)

platform.t: Defends H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act) for no tax on tips and overtime, an expanded/permanent child tax credit and small-business investment incentives; opposes higher taxes.

Says the law's work and reporting requirements target 'waste, fraud, and abuse' and protect the programs; says he fought steeper Medicaid cuts in earlier drafts and backed the $50B rural hospital fund.
Defended starting the 2026 war so Iran cannot get nuclear weapons; opposed ground troops and opposed war-powers limits; said in May 2026 the war was 'very close to being over.'
Supports border security legislation; reportedly open to protections for people brought here as children; supported White House handing the Minnesota enforcement operation to Tom Homan.
Praised Dobbs; opposes a nationwide ban; supports Arizona's 15-week law; criticized the 2024 ruling reviving the 1864 ban.
Co-signed a May 2025 letter warning against Trump administration plans to downsize the Social Security Administration.

promises.t: Keep cutting taxes and oppose new taxes (2026 debate).

claims.claim: First naturalized American citizen from Mexico elected to the U.S. House from Arizona.

said.where: official House bio; repeated in Clean Elections debate

record.t: KTAR reported the same distinction (Mar. 2023). No contrary record found; no primary roster was checked.

claims.claim: First in his family to graduate from college.

record.t: Repeated by Wikipedia and KTAR, both relying on his own account; he does hold a University of Arizona B.A.

claims.claim: Named the most bipartisan member from Arizona by the Center for Effective Lawmaking and the Lugar Center (first term); in the debate, 'independently ranked the most bipartisan in Arizona every year.'

said.where: official House bio; Clean Elections debate

record.t: The Lugar Center and CEL rankings were not opened.

claims.claim: Backed a $50 billion rural hospital fund in H.R. 1.

record.t: The law includes a $50B rural hospital fund; KFF estimates it offsets about a third of projected rural Medicaid losses. Arizona received $167M in the first tranche, $33M below its request.

claims.claim: The Medicaid changes target waste, fraud and abuse and don't affect those who most need the program.

said.where: Tucson business roundtable; repeated at 2026 debate

record.t: CBO estimated the House bill would cut federal Medicaid spending about $700B and leave at least 8.6M more people uninsured, mostly through work requirements and eligibility checks, not fraud findings. In Arizona about half a million people lost SNAP benefits amid processing problems (3M+ dropped calls), which KJZZ says points more to paperwork hurdles than fraud.

said.where: Live The Dream Media radio interview

record.t: Rested on her original 2025 disclosure listing a $1M–$5M consulting-firm stake; her amended and 2026 reports put the stake at $50K–$100K and her net worth between about –$310K and $336K. The firm was a political consultancy; no lobbying registration was cited.

claims.claim: 'Every law enforcement organization endorsed me and endorsed against my opponent.'

record.t: No endorsement roster for law-enforcement groups was found.

claims.claim: Mendoza supports raising taxes while not paying her own, and is tied to lobbying and dark money.

record.t: No tax lien or unpaid-tax record was found in sources opened; her disclosures list no tax liabilities.

said.t: Co-signed a letter to Speaker Johnson saying signers 'cannot and will not support' a bill with any reduction in Medicaid coverage for vulnerable populations.

did.t: Voted for H.R. 1, which CBO said would cut Medicaid about $700B and cost at least 8.6M people coverage. He says the coverage losses fall on non-needy adults, not vulnerable groups; critics say he broke the pledge. The record shows the vote and CBO estimates; who counts as 'vulnerable' is the disputed point.

said.t: Said he would oppose legislation limiting Trump's authority to wage war on Iran.

did.t: Voted against the Iran war powers resolution (Wikipedia; roll call in key-votes file).

promises_prev.promise: Secure the border ('Arizona's border should be an asset, not a liability').

evidence.t: Co-sponsored the Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act, which passed the House in Feb. 2025; voted for H.R. 1, which included about $170B for DHS.

complicating.t: Border outcomes depend on executive enforcement; the officer-safety bill's Senate fate was not checked.

promises_prev.promise: Reduce government spending to fight inflation and high housing costs.

evidence.t: Voted for H.R. 1, which cut federal Medicaid spending (~$700–800B) but which CBO estimated would raise deficits about $3.8T, mainly from tax cuts.

complicating.t: Net effect on total federal spending was not established in sources opened; deficit and spending are different measures.

entries.t: 2022–2024: praised Dobbs, opposed a national ban, backed Arizona's 15-week limit, criticized the 1864-law ruling.
2024: declined to say whether he supported ACA repeal.

note.t: Modest holdings: state pension, two Wells Fargo business accounts, his wife's IRA in index funds, joint index ETFs and Treasury bonds, and his wife's consulting firm Two Worlds Branding LLC (S-corp income $5K–$15K). Privately sponsored travel: Republican Main Street Partnership paid for an April 11–18, 2025 trip to Crete and Athens, Greece, and a Sept. 2025 trip to Amelia Island, Fla. The 2025 report was filed July 14, 2026 under an extension.

legal.t: His 2025 annual report shows a joint Aug. 28, 2025 purchase of a U.S. Treasury bond ($15,001–$50,000) and two ETFs, reported only in the annual filed July 14, 2026; no periodic transaction report appears in his filings. The Copper Courier, citing House Ethics guidance that Treasury purchases likely require a PTR within 45 days, called it an apparent STOCK Act violation.
